subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the equation of the circle passing through the point (0, −3) and cutting the circles x² + y² − 6x + 3y + 5 = 0, x² + y² − x − 7y = 0 orthogonally.

mark_split.label: Set up the circle and use the point
Solve for g, f, c and write the circle

insider_note: Three unknowns (g, f, c) need exactly three equations here — the given point supplies one, and each orthogonality condition supplies one more; solve them as a genuine simultaneous system, not by guessing which to substitute first.

steps.label: Set up the circle and use the point
steps.margin_note: First mark. This point is not the origin, so c does not vanish — it stays linked to f through this equation.
steps.why: Substituting the given point into the general circle's own equation gives one linear relation between the three unknowns g, f, c — here it links f and c directly, since the point has no x-coordinate.
common_mistakes: Substituting x = −3, y = 0 by mixing up the coordinate order.
steps.memory_tip: A point with x = 0 always removes g from its equation, leaving only f and c linked together.

steps.label: Apply the first orthogonal condition
steps.margin_note: Second mark. g′ = −3, f′ = 3/2, c′ = 5 from the first given circle.
lines: S is orthogonal to x² + y² − 6x + 3y + 5 = 0
steps.why: The standard orthogonality test 2gg′ + 2ff′ = c + c′, applied to the first circle, is the second of the three equations needed to pin down g, f, c.
common_mistakes: Reading f′ as 3 instead of 3/2 — it is half the coefficient of y, not the coefficient itself.
Moving c to the wrong side, changing its sign.
steps.memory_tip: Every orthogonality equation has the SAME shape: 2gg′ + 2ff′ − c − c′ = 0 — write it the same way each time to avoid sign slips.

steps.label: Apply the second orthogonal condition
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The second circle has c″ = 0, since it has no constant term.
lines: S is orthogonal to x² + y² − x − 7y = 0
steps.why: The orthogonality test applied to the second circle is the third and final equation needed — three equations for three unknowns g, f, c.
common_mistakes: Missing that c″ = 0 because this circle has no constant term, and writing an extra unknown on the right.
Sign error turning −g − 7f − c = 0 into the wrong form for elimination.
steps.memory_tip: No constant term in a circle's equation always means that circle's own c is 0 in the orthogonality formula.

steps.label: Solve for g, f, c and write the circle
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Combine (1), (2), (3) as one simultaneous system, then substitute back.
lines: Substituting g, f, c in S = 0,
steps.why: Combining the three linear equations (1), (2), (3) by elimination solves for g, f, c uniquely; substituting them back into the general circle gives the one circle meeting the point condition and both orthogonality conditions.
common_mistakes: Solving the pair (4) and (5) in the wrong order and mixing up which unknown is eliminated first.
Forgetting to multiply the final equation by 3 to clear the fractions in 2g and 2f.
steps.memory_tip: Three unknowns need three equations, solved together — never substitute one equation into itself twice by mistake.
